absent: Exact behavior of sleep primitives invoked while unlocked, including remaining-time accounting and spurious-wakeup handling.
Implementations of variable and bit wake operations and of automatically removing and bit wake callbacks.
Implementations of out-of-line bit waiters and of ordinary, io and timeout wait actions.
Mapping from a variable address to its wait queue and initialization performed for variable wait entries beyond exclusivity.
Layouts of generic wait queue heads and entries, task and signal structures, and task state values.
Full automatic-group and task-group layouts, root group contents and global group-lock scope.
Implementations of group creation, online transition, deferred unregistration and real-time group cleanup.
Scheduler policy semantics, priority ranges and deadline parameter validation beyond numeric identifiers and field order.
Trace event payloads and emission points for scheduler and extensible-scheduler subsystems.
Ordering guarantees of bit and atomic primitives beyond the acquire, release and barrier usage shown in these fragments.

findings.text: The lane exposes a family of queue-head wait helpers that evaluate a caller condition on entry and sleep only when the condition is not yet satisfied. The family distinguishes an uninterruptible form, interruptible forms that report interruption status and optionally run a caller hook while unlocked, and time-bounded forms that start from a caller timeout and report the remaining time. All forms coordinate with a caller-owned spinlock held with interrupts disabled across the decision to sleep.

The lane exposes bit-based sleep entry points that wait for a single bit inside a caller word to change state. Variants cover ordinary sleep, io flavoured sleep, bounded-time sleep, caller-supplied action sleep, and lock-acquisition sleep that attempts an atomic set first. All variants are documented as sleepable and take a caller mode argument that selects the sleep state.

The lane exposes address-based variable wait helpers that sleep on a queue derived from a caller variable address until a caller condition becomes true. Variants cover ordinary sleep, io sleep, killable sleep, interruptible sleep, bounded-time sleep, and sleeps that drop a caller spinlock or mutex while sleeping. Outer wrappers check the condition once before entering the queuing loop and report interruption or remaining time where applicable.

The lane exposes small wake helpers that publish a state change and then wake waiters on the same object. They cover clearing a bit with release ordering followed by a wake, test-and-clear with conditional wake, decrement-and-test of a count with conditional variable wake, release-store of a value with barrier and wake, and protected variable wakes that require the caller to already hold an associated lock.

A bit-wait key carries a pointer to the flag word under observation, an integer bit index within that word, and a timeout value. A bit-wait queue element pairs such a key with a generic wait queue entry, allowing variable and bit waits to reuse the generic queuing machinery while retaining the observed word and bit.

The clone argument block is an ordered sequence of eleven 64-bit aligned fields for flags, pid file descriptor location, child thread identifier location, parent thread identifier location, exit signal number, stack address, stack size, thread-local storage descriptor, thread identifier array pointer, array length, and cgroup descriptor.

The scheduling attribute block begins with a size field followed by policy and flags, then a signed nice value for normal and batch classes, an unsigned priority for fifo and round-robin classes, three 64-bit deadline parameters for runtime deadline and period, and two 32-bit utilization hints for minimum and maximum. Size identifies which suffix is present.

Exit-signal selection uses the low eight bits. The next low-word flags are single-bit creation controls with decimal values 256, 512, 1024, 2048, 4096, 8192, 16384, 32768, 65536, 131072, 262144, 524288, 1048576, 2097152, 4194304, 8388608, 16777216, 33554432, 67108864, 134217728, 268435456, 536870912, 1073741824 and 2147483648 in the documented order from virtual-memory sharing through io context sharing.

Extended creation controls live above 32 bits as powers of two for bit positions 32 through 36, plus a further control at bit position 37 for an empty mount namespace. A time-namespace creation control reuses the low-byte decimal value 128, and an unshare control for an empty mount namespace uses decimal value 1048576.
Published clone argument sizes are 64 bytes for version zero, 80 bytes for version one and 88 bytes for version two.

Scheduling policies are numbered zero for normal, one for fifo, two for round-robin, three for batch, five for idle, six for deadline and seven for extensible scheduling. A separate reset-on-fork control uses decimal bit value 1073741824.

Scheduling attribute flags use low-byte decimal bits one, two, four, eight, sixteen, thirty-two and sixty-four for reset on fork, reclaim, deadline overrun, keep policy, keep parameters, minimum clamp and maximum clamp. Keep-all combines keep policy with keep parameters, utilization clamp combines the two clamp bits, and the all mask combines reset, reclaim, overrun, keep-all and clamp. Deadline dynamic reporting uses value one.
Published scheduling attribute sizes are 48 bytes for version zero and 56 bytes for version one, where the extension adds the two utilization hint fields.
Deadline tracing distinguishes four server kinds numbered zero through three for other, task, fair server and external server. Tracing subsystems are named sched and sched_ext.

Queue-entry constructors bind a new entry to the calling task, install a wake callback, initialize list linkage and clear flags. The default constructor selects an automatically removing wake callback, while the functional form accepts a caller-supplied callback. Reinitialization repeats the same binding for an existing entry.

Bit-wait constructors bind a queue element to the calling task, select the bit-wake callback, initialize list linkage and record the observed word and bit index through a key initializer. The initializer records only the word pointer and bit number, leaving remaining key state to the caller.

Balancing skip reporting enumerates seven causes for unsuitable, shared read-only, inaccessible, scan delay, inactive identifier, ignored identifier and completed sequence. Supporting macros have dual expansions that either declare enumeration values or build value-to-label table entries, and scheduler-statistics event macros toggle between active event definitions and disabled no-operation definitions.

Scheduler switch tracing requires the examined task to be the calling task. Preempted tasks are reported with a dedicated running-report maximum regardless of stored state, because preemption does not dequeue based on state. Other tasks derive a report value from a state index combined with exit state, mapping index zero to zero and any higher index to a single bit selected by one less than the index.

Automatic grouping is enabled by default and exposed through a kernel control named for autogroup enablement with unsigned-integer range zero to one. Initialization wires the initial task signal structure to a default group object, initializes its reference count and reader-writer semaphore, and registers the control. A disabled configuration replaces registration with an empty operation.

Variable waits progress through queue preparation on the address-derived queue, condition test with immediate completion when true, interruption check that reports pending signals for interruptible states, execution of a caller sleep primitive, and repetition until success or interruption. Completion always removes the element from the queue before reporting the outcome, and timeout forms carry remaining time through iterations.

Automatic groups live under reference counting with explicit get and put operations. Sampling a task group prefers the task signal group under protection and falls back to the default group when protection cannot be taken. Creation allocates a group object and a child scheduling group, initializes counting and locking, assigns a fresh sequence identifier, links the two objects and brings the scheduling group online. Destruction detaches real-time state where applicable and then releases and destroys the scheduling group. Releasing the owning task-group wrapper frees the linked automatic group.

Scheduling-group teardown separates logical release from deferred destruction. Release removes the group from global and sibling lists under protection so later tree walks cannot discover it, with actual unregistration deferred until after a grace period. Destruction schedules reclamation through a read-copy-update callback.

Interrupt-protected waits enter with the caller spinlock held with interrupts disabled, validate the condition, and only then drop the lock around the actual sleep, reacquiring the same protection immediately after waking. Bounded-time forms preserve the timeout across the drop and reacquire. Generic variable waits apply the same drop-sleep-reacquire pattern to a caller lock of parameterized type, selecting uninterruptible sleep for spinlock and mutex wrappers.

Task-group sampling holds the target signal-hand lock while copying the group reference. Group release holds a global task-group spinlock with interrupt state saved while unlinking lists. Protected variable wakes assert through lock validation that the caller already holds the associated guard. Bit-clear wakes clear with unlock semantics and a post-atomic barrier before waking, while test-clear, decrement-test and release-store wakes rely on the documented ordering of their own atomic primitive plus an explicit barrier where stated.

Bit-wait entry points first probe the observed bit and return success immediately when the bit is already clear, or attempt an atomic set and succeed immediately when the bit was clear for lock-acquisition forms. Only when the fast probe indicates contention do they delegate to an out-of-line waiter with a selected wait action and caller mode. Timeout forms additionally forward the caller timeout.

Boot initialization establishes the default automatic group for the initial task. Group-wrapper release frees the linked automatic group. Scheduling-group release and destroy provide the unlink and deferred-reclaim steps used during teardown. Runtime sampling and creation helpers provide reference-counted lookup and on-demand group instantiation with fallback to the default group on allocation failure.

All bit and variable waits may sleep and must not be entered from atomic context. Interruptible and killable forms can return early with a signal indication and require callers to handle partial waits, while uninterruptible and io forms do not report signals. Timeout forms return remaining time with zero meaning expiry, so callers must distinguish expiry from early satisfaction of the condition. Locks must be held on entry where documented and are not held across the sleep itself.

Automatic-group creation can fail during object or scheduling-group allocation and then logs a rate-limited warning and returns a reference to the default group instead of failing the caller. Callers therefore cannot assume a fresh identity after creation and must handle aliasing to the default group. Sequence numbers come from an atomic counter.

Header guards protect bit-wait, scheduler-event, extensible-scheduler-event and user-visible scheduling headers against multiple inclusion. Callback types describe a task visitor returning an integer status from a task pointer and opaque argument, and a bit-wait action returning an integer status from a key pointer and mode.
